learn.title: Geothermal Energy: Tapping Earth's Inner Heat
learn.intro: Geothermal energy harnesses the Earth's internal heat to generate clean, reliable electricity and heating. Unlike solar or wind, it provides baseload power 24/7. With vast potential globally, geothermal reduces dependence on fossil fuels while offering stable, low-carbon energy for communities and industries.
learn.c1_text: India has significant geothermal reserves, especially in the Himalayan region and parts of Rajasthan. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has identified 342 hot/spring locations. While commercial plants are still emerging, pilot projects aim to harness 10 GW by 2030 as part of India’s clean energy push.
learn.c2_text: There are three main types: high-temperature resources for large-scale power plants, low-temperature sources for direct heating, and enhanced geothermal systems that inject water into dry rock. The U.S. leads in geothermal electricity production, generating over 3.7 GW annually—enough for 3.5 million homes.
learn.stat1: India targets 10 GW geothermal capacity by 2030
learn.stat2: Global geothermal potential: over 200 GW technically feasible
learn.stat3: Geothermal plants operate at 90% capacity factor—higher than solar or wind
learn.stat4: Iceland generates nearly 25% of its total electricity from geothermal

learn.title: Second Life EV Batteries for Grid Storage
learn.intro: Electric vehicle batteries retain up to 80% of their original capacity after retirement from cars. Repurposing them as stationary storage extends their life, reduces waste, and supports grid stability. This circular economy approach maximizes value from expensive battery materials while accelerating renewable integration.
learn.c1_title: 🔋 Retired EV Batteries Get a New Job
learn.c1_text: When EV batteries drop below 80% capacity, they’re no longer ideal for vehicles but still excellent for storing solar or wind energy at home or on the grid. Think of it like reusing an old laptop battery for a flashlight—it’s not top-tier anymore, but it still powers your needs effectively.
learn.c2_text: Repurposed EV batteries can store excess solar power generated during the day and release it during peak evening demand. A typical Nissan Leaf battery (24 kWh) can power an average Indian household for nearly two days. These systems help smooth out intermittency issues in renewable-dominant grids.
learn.c3_text: India’s Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme promotes EV adoption, creating future battery waste streams. Startups like Attero and Li-Cycle are developing recycling and reuse technologies. The government aims to make India a global hub for EV manufacturing and sustainable battery management by 2030.
learn.stat1: Retired EV batteries retain 70-80% of original capacity
learn.stat2: Global second-life battery market projected to reach $7.8 billion by 2030
learn.stat3: One Nissan Leaf battery can store enough energy for 2 average Indian homes daily
learn.stat4: India plans to deploy 30 million EVs by 2030 under FAME scheme

learn.title: Concentrated Solar Power: Mirrors Make Electricity
learn.intro: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) uses mirrors to focus sunlight onto a receiver, generating intense heat that drives turbines. Unlike photovoltaics, CSP can store thermal energy for hours, enabling electricity generation even after sunset. This makes it a powerful tool for reliable, dispatchable solar power.
learn.c1_title: 🌞 Focusing Sunbeams Like a Magnifying Glass
learn.c1_text: CSP works like a giant magnifying glass—mirrors called heliostats track the sun and reflect light onto a central tower. The concentrated heat (over 500°C) warms a fluid that produces steam to turn turbines. It’s similar to using a magnifying glass to start a fire, but scaled up to power entire cities.
learn.c2_text: CSP plants often use molten salt to store heat for up to 15 hours. When the sun sets, stored thermal energy continues producing steam, allowing electricity generation well into the night. This built-in storage capability gives CSP a major advantage over traditional solar panels that stop working when dark.
learn.c3_title: 🇮🇳 India’s CSP Ambitions in Gujarat and Rajasthan
learn.c3_text: India has identified over 10 GW of CSP potential, particularly in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh. The 100 MW CSP plant in Rajasthan’s Jodhpur district is among Asia’s largest. Under the National Solar Mission, India plans to expand CSP capacity significantly to meet its 500 GW renewable target by 2030.
learn.stat1: CSP can store thermal energy for up to 15 hours
learn.stat2: Global CSP capacity reached 6.8 GW by 2023
learn.stat3: CSP plants achieve 40-50% efficiency in converting heat to electricity
learn.stat4: India has identified over 10 GW of technically feasible CSP potential

learn.title: Hydrogen Colors: Blue, Green, and Grey Explained
learn.intro: Hydrogen isn’t a fuel itself—it’s an energy carrier that must be produced. Its environmental impact depends on how it’s made: grey from fossil fuels, blue with carbon capture, and green from renewables. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for evaluating hydrogen’s role in decarbonizing hard-to-electrify sectors like steel and shipping.
learn.c1_text: The colors represent production methods. Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas without capturing emissions. Blue adds carbon capture to reduce CO₂ release. Green uses electrolysis powered by renewables—zero emissions. Think of it like coffee: black (grey), with cream (blue), or plant-based milk (green)—same base, different environmental footprints.
learn.c2_title: 🏭 How Each Type Is Made Matters
learn.c2_text: Grey hydrogen dominates today, made via steam methane reforming—producing 9 kg of CO₂ per kg of hydrogen. Blue captures 60-90% of that CO₂. Green hydrogen splits water using renewable-powered electrolyzers but costs 2-4x more. As renewables get cheaper, green hydrogen becomes economically competitive.
learn.c3_text: Launched in 2023, India’s $2.3 billion National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to make the country a global hub for green hydrogen production and export. Targeting 5 MMT annual production by 2030, it focuses on sectors like steel, chemicals, and transportation. Major investments planned in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu industrial corridors.
learn.stat1: Green hydrogen costs $3-6/kg; grey hydrogen costs $1-2/kg
learn.stat2: Global hydrogen demand: 94 million tonnes annually (2023)
learn.stat3: India targets 5 MMT green hydrogen production by 2030
learn.stat4: Steam methane reforming produces 9 kg CO₂ per kg of grey hydrogen

learn.title: HVDC Transmission: Moving Power Over Long Distances
learn.intro: High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) transmission lines efficiently move massive amounts of electricity across continents with minimal losses. Unlike alternating current, DC power can travel thousands of kilometers without significant energy degradation. HVDC enables cross-border energy trading and connects remote renewable sources to demand centers.
learn.c1_title: ⚡ Why DC Beats AC Over Long Distances
learn.c1_text: Alternating current (AC) loses energy over long distances due to inductance and capacitance effects. HVDC avoids these issues, losing only ~3% per 1,000 km. Think of it like water in pipes—AC is like turbulent flow causing friction loss, while DC is smooth laminar flow with minimal resistance over distance.
learn.c2_text: China’s ±1100 kV UHVDC transmission line spans 3,324 km, delivering 12 GW—enough for 30 million people. The NordLink cable connects Norway’s hydroelectric dams to Germany’s grid across 623 km of seabed. These superhighways for electrons enable countries to share renewable energy resources efficiently.
learn.c3_title: 🇮🇳 India’s Green Energy Corridor and HVDC Plans
learn.c3_text: India is building HVDC links to evacuate renewable energy from resource-rich states. The ±800 kV Raigarh-Pugalur line transmits 6 GW across 1,465 km. Plans include a ±1200 kV line and cross-border connections with Bangladesh and Nepal. These projects support India’s goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
learn.stat1: HVDC loses only 3% energy per 1,000 km vs 7% for AC
learn.stat2: China’s 3,324 km Changji-Guquan line transmits 12 GW
learn.stat3: India plans 40 GW of HVDC transmission capacity by 2030
learn.stat4: NordLink cable connects Norway and Germany across 623 km seabed

learn.title: Iron-Air Batteries: 100+ Hour Energy Storage
learn.intro: Iron-air batteries offer revolutionary long-duration energy storage lasting 100+ hours—far beyond lithium-ion’s few hours. Using abundant iron, they provide weeks of backup power at a fraction of current costs. This technology could finally solve renewable intermittency, enabling grids powered entirely by wind and solar.
learn.c1_text: Iron-air batteries store energy by rusting iron during discharge and reversing the process during charging—like a controlled corrosion cycle. They use cheap, abundant materials: iron powder, air, and water. Unlike lithium-ion, they don’t degrade quickly and can remain discharged for months without damage.
learn.c2_text: Form Energy’s iron-air system costs $20-40/kWh—10x cheaper than lithium-ion for long-duration storage. Each unit stores energy for 100+ hours, enough to power a home through two weeks of cloudy, windless weather. The technology uses 100x less lithium and cobalt than conventional batteries.
learn.c3_text: India’s grid requires massive long-duration storage to integrate its ambitious renewable targets. With plans for 500 GW renewables by 2030, India needs storage solutions beyond 4-hour lithium systems. Iron-air batteries could provide affordable seasonal storage, especially critical for states like Rajasthan and Gujarat with high solar penetration.
learn.stat1: Iron-air batteries cost $20-40/kWh—10x cheaper than lithium-ion
learn.stat2: Can store energy for 100+ hours vs 4-6 hours for lithium-ion
learn.stat3: Use 100x less lithium and cobalt than conventional batteries
